**Data that changes over time.** For fraud or churn, dealing examples out like cards mixes future data into training. The model then "sees the future" and scores look better than real life. Instead, split by time: train on older months and test on the next month, then roll forward.

**Related examples.** If one customer has many rows, some can land in training and others in testing. The model memorises that customer, which is a form of **leakage** (test information sneaking into training). Keep each customer's rows together in one fold.

**LLM or RAG apps.** You usually don't train these, so there is nothing to retrain per fold. Instead, build a fixed set of test questions with expected answers. Score every version on that same set, and log each version as an MLflow run.

learn:term.a:
**Folds** are the pieces. **Cross-validation** is the method that uses those pieces.

A **fold** is just a group of examples. You split your data into a few equal groups, often 5. On their own, folds do nothing. They are just piles.

**Cross-validation** is the whole process. It takes turns: each fold gets one round as the test set, while all the other folds are used for training. Every round gives a score. At the end you report the average score and how much the scores vary (the **standard deviation**, a measure of spread).

An everyday comparison: folds are like dividing a class into 5 study groups. Cross-validation is the rotation where each group takes a turn presenting while the others listen.

In the lesson's example, 10 examples become 5 folds: fold 0 holds examples 0 and 5, fold 1 holds 1 and 6, and so on. That's the splitting. Then cross-validation runs 5 rounds. Round 1 tests on fold 0 and trains on folds 1 to 4. Round 2 tests on fold 1, and so on. That gives 5 scores.

So you need folds to do cross-validation. Cross-validation is what turns them into a fair test.

judge.notes: No major problem; the 'presenting while others listen' analogy is loose, since the presenting group is the test set, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Ship it: the quality win is clear”?
check:0:0.a:
"Ship it" gets one thing right. The quality win really is clear. The new version won 15 questions and lost 5. That gap of 10 is bigger than twice the square root of 20, which is about 9. So the paired check would say "better".

But that check never gets a turn. The rule runs the **gates** first. A gate is a must-hold condition: fail it and the answer is no. A failing must-pass case is a gate failure. Those cases are there because getting them wrong is not acceptable, however good the rest looks.

"Ship it" lets a strong quality score make up for a broken must-pass case. That is the trap the lesson warns about: picking the number that favours the version you hoped would win. Gates cannot be traded away. Think of the job offer again: a great title does not help if the salary is below your minimum.

The saved reason would read "must-pass case failed". The team fixes it, then runs the comparison again.

"Keep the baseline: a gate failed" is better because the fixed order checks gates first, and any failed gate ends the decision before quality is weighed.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Too close to call: one case is not much”?
check:0:2.a:
"Too close to call" gets one thing right: it does not ship the new version. But it reaches that answer for the wrong reason.

"Too close to call" belongs to the quality step. It means the wins and losses are too even to tell which version is better. That step only runs after every gate passes.

A must-pass case is a **gate**: something that must hold, or the answer is no. Gates are not weighed against anything. One failure is enough. It does not matter how small it looks, or how strong the quality win is. That is the point of writing the rule down first. It stops you from talking yourself past a failure because the other numbers look good.

Calling it "too close to call" also sends the team the wrong way. They would gather more examples or argue about cost, when the real job is to fix that one failing case.

"Keep the baseline: a gate failed" is better because it follows the rule in order. It also records the true reason, so a reviewer knows exactly what to fix.

judge.notes: No substantive problems. The closing part runs two sentences where the brief asked for one, which is a minor style slip.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Only the first gate that failed”?
check:1:0.a:
"Only the first gate that failed" gets one thing right: the decision itself. A gate is a must-hold check, so one failure is enough to say "keep baseline". Stopping early would not change the answer.

What it misses is the reasons. The report is not just for the decision. It tells the team what to fix.

Picture it. The report says only "cost over budget". The team spends a week making the version cheaper. They run the comparison again, and now it says "must-pass case fails". That problem was there all along. The report just hid it. Now they need a second round of fixing and re-running that could have been avoided.

It also misleads the reviewer, and you in six months. Anyone reading the saved reasons would think cost was the only issue.

So checking every gate costs almost nothing extra. It walks through the three gates once instead of stopping partway. And it saves whole rounds of work.

"Both failed gates" is better because it gives the same decision plus the full list of problems, so the team can fix them all in one round.

judge.notes: No real problems. One minor point: the story has a report that shows only 'cost over budget', but in the lesson's listed gate order the must-pass check comes first, so the hidden failure would more naturally be cost.

check:1:2.a:
"The quality score first" gets one thing right. Quality does matter, and it is part of the rule. But it comes later, and only if every gate passes.

Here two gates have already failed. Cost is over budget, and a must-pass case fails. A gate is a hard yes-or-no check. If any gate fails, the answer is "keep baseline", however good the quality looks. So the quality score cannot change the decision. The rule says not to even run the paired check.

Leading with quality also causes two problems:

- **It invites cherry-picking.** A strong quality number at the top makes it tempting to excuse the failures. That is exactly what a fixed rule, written before you run anything, is meant to stop.
- **It hides what to fix.** The team needs the list of failed gates, not a score that does not count yet.

"Both failed gates" is better because the report should name every gate that failed, cost and the must-pass case, so the team can fix both in one round.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Ship it: every gate passed”?
check:2:0.a:
"Ship it: every gate passed" gets one thing right. All the gates did pass, so the new version is allowed to compete. Nothing rules it out.

What it misses is that the gates only decide whether the new version gets to be judged on quality. Passing them doesn't make it better. Think of the job offer again. A salary that clears your minimum gets the offer considered. It doesn't mean you take it.

After the gates comes the paired check. Here the gap between wins and losses wasn't big enough to count. So you have no clear evidence the new version answers questions better than the old one. Shipping anyway means swapping something proven for something unproven, with no clear gain.

"Too close to call" has a fixed meaning in the rule. You keep the baseline for now. Then you either gather more examples to get a clearer answer, or decide on cost instead. You also save the reasons, so a reviewer can see why.

"Keep the baseline for now" is better because a change should have to show it's better before it replaces what already works, and here it hasn't.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Drop the new version for good”?
check:2:1.a:
"Drop the new version for good" gets one thing right. You don't ship it today. The baseline (the version already in use) stays in place.

What it misses is what "too close to call" means. It does not mean the new version lost. It means the gap between its wins and losses was too small to say either way. The new version might be a little better, a little worse, or the same. You just can't tell yet.

Dropping it for good treats "we don't know" as "it's worse." Only the other result, where losses minus wins is big enough, earns that verdict. A close result leaves real options open. You can run more examples, since a bigger test can show a gap that a small one hides. Or, since every gate passed, you can choose on cost. If the new version is cheaper at about the same quality, that may be a good reason to pick it.

"Keep the baseline for now" is better because it plays it safe today while leaving room to decide later, once you have more evidence.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Gates first, then one test” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "When I compare two versions, I get several numbers: quality, must-pass cases, cost and speed. If I read each one alone, I can usually find one that favours the version I hoped would win."

*The idea.* "So I write one decision rule before I run anything. First come the gates, the hard limits: must-pass cases, cost per task, and p95 latency, the time that 95 out of 100 requests beat. If any gate fails, the answer is keep the baseline, and I list every failure so the team can fix them all at once. Only if every gate passes do I compare quality, with one paired test on the same examples. The result is ship, keep baseline, or too close to call."

*A trade-off.* "A big quality win can't rescue a blown budget. That feels strict, but it stops us arguing after we've seen the results."

**A likely follow-up**

"What do you do when it's too close to call?"

*Hint:* Keep the baseline for now. Then gather more examples, or choose on cost. Add that you save the reasons with the decision, so a reviewer can see why.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs the rule was skipped or done wrong**

- **The reason to ship keeps changing.** One week it's "quality went up". The next it's "it's cheaper". That usually means someone picked whichever number looked best after seeing the results.
- **Surprises after release.** Users complain it feels slow, or the bill jumps. A gate (a must-hold check like cost or speed) was probably never checked.
- **Fixes come in drips.** A version is rejected for being slow. It gets fixed, then rejected again for cost. The check stopped at the first failing gate instead of listing them all.
- **A "win" that fades.** It shipped on a small quality edge, then scores drop back in real use. The paired check (wins versus losses on the same questions) was skipped, or the gap was too small to count.
- **Bare decisions.** A log says "ship" with no reasons and no link to the evaluation run.

**Quickest check**

Open the saved decision records for your last few releases in MLflow. For each one, confirm three things:

1. The rule was written before the evaluation ran. Compare the timestamps.
2. Every gate shows its value next to its budget.
3. The wins-minus-losses arithmetic holds up when you redo it by hand.

judge.notes: The answer is sound, but it runs about 200 words, and the 'compare the timestamps' check is vague because the lesson's saved record has no time for when the rule was written.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Very little data.** With only a handful of questions where the versions disagree, the paired check almost never finds a clear winner. You will keep getting "too close to call." Add more examples first, or agree up front to decide on cost when quality is a tie.

**2. Users or data change over time.** This is called drift: today's questions stop looking like the ones in your test set. A decision that was right last spring may be wrong now. Refresh the test set from recent real requests and run the same rule again. The saved reasons tell you why the old decision was made, so you can see whether that reasoning still holds.

**3. An LLM grades the answers.** In LLM or RAG apps (RAG means the model looks up documents before answering), another model often judges right or wrong. That judge makes mistakes, which makes the wins and losses less trustworthy. Use the same judge for both versions, and check a sample of its grades by hand.

judge.notes: Minor: point 2 runs to four sentences against the 2-3 asked for, and 'LLM' is not spelled out. Neither breaks a listed check.

learn:term.q: How is “ship” different from “keep the baseline”?
learn:term.a:
The decision has three possible outcomes. Two of them are the opposites you are asking about.

**Ship** means you release the new version to users. It replaces the old one.

**Keep the baseline** means the old version (the "baseline", the one already running) stays, and the new one does not go out.

The third, **too close to call**, also keeps the baseline for now. It means you need more examples, or you choose on cost.

Ship has to be earned. First come the **gates**: checks that must all hold, or the answer is no. Then comes the **paired check**. On the same questions, count the ones only the new version got right (wins) and the ones only the old version got right (losses). You ship when every gate passes and wins are clearly ahead. You keep the baseline when any gate fails, or when losses are clearly ahead.

It's like replacing your phone. You switch only if the new one fits your budget and is clearly better.

In the lesson's example, the p95 latency was 2.1 s against a 1.5 s budget. (p95 means 95 out of 100 requests are faster than this.) One gate failed. So the answer is keep baseline, because: too slow.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Yes: 4 points is a clear gain”?
check:0:0.a:
"Yes: 4 points is a clear gain" gets one thing right. Prompt B really did score 4 points higher on this eval set. That is a real result, and it might hint that B is better.

What it misses is the margin of error. That is how far a measured score could be from the true score, just by luck of which questions ended up in the set. With 100 questions, the margin is about 10 points either way. So a measured 70 could really be anywhere from about 60 to 80.

Both prompts carry that wobble. A 4-point gap is much smaller than 10 points. Chance alone could easily produce it, even if A and B are equally good. Calling it "clear" treats a rough guess as the truth.

To show a gap that small, you would need more examples. Or you could compare A and B on the same examples, which later lessons show is more sensitive.

"Not on its own: the gap is inside the margin" is better because it sees that a 4-point difference fits inside the roughly 10-point wobble of a 100-question eval set, so it cannot prove B is better.

check:0:2.q: Why not “No: an eval can't compare two prompts”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. A 4-point gap on 100 questions is not good evidence that prompt B is better. Being cautious here is correct.

But its reason is wrong. Comparing two prompts is exactly what an eval is for. The trouble here is the size of this eval set, not evals in general.

With 100 questions, each score could be about 10 points off either way. That range is the **margin of error**. A 4-point gap is well inside it, so random luck in which questions you picked could explain the whole difference.

Change the setup and the same kind of eval can settle the question:

- **More examples.** With 1,600 questions the margin shrinks to about 2.5 points. A real 4-point gap would then stand out.
- **The same examples for both prompts.** This is a more sensitive comparison, covered later in this module.

"No: an eval can't compare two prompts" would rule out all of these, which is too strong.

"Not on its own: the gap is inside the margin" is better because it names the real problem, too few examples for a gap this small. That points you to the fix instead of giving up on evals.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Yes, any change will show up”?
check:1:0.a:
"Yes, any change will show up" gets one thing right. If you change your prompt and rerun, the score number may well move. You will see a different pass rate on the screen.

What it misses is whether that movement means anything. With only 25 questions, the margin of error is about 20 points either way. The margin of error is how far your measured score could be from the real pass rate, just by luck of which questions you happened to pick. So a score of 70% could really be anywhere from about 50% to 90%.

A 3-point gain is tiny next to that 20-point wobble. The score could go up or down by more than 3 points from chance alone, even if your change did nothing. You couldn't tell a real improvement from noise.

There's also a simpler problem. With 25 questions, each one is worth 4 points. A 3-point change is less than a single question flipping.

"No, the margin of error is too wide" is better because it compares the hoped-for gain to the margin and sees that the gain is far smaller.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Yes, if you run it twice”?
check:1:2.a:
"Yes, if you run it twice" has a sensible instinct behind it. AI models can give slightly different answers each time, so running again shows you how much the score wobbles from run to run. That is worth knowing.

But it misses where the big uncertainty comes from. The margin of error here is not mainly about the model's mood on a given run. It is about having only 25 questions. Those 25 are a small sample of all the questions your users might ask. A different set of 25 could easily score quite differently.

Running the same 25 questions twice does not give you 50 examples. It gives you the same 25 examples, checked twice. The sample is still tiny.

With 25 questions, the margin is about plus or minus 20 points. A 3-point improvement is buried inside that range. You can't tell a real gain from luck. Even 400 questions only gets you down to about 5 points.

"No, the margin of error is too wide" is better because it names the real limit: 25 examples give about ±20 points, far more than the 3-point change you hope to see.

check:2:1.a:
"About 200 questions" gets one thing right. More questions do shrink the margin of error, which is how far your measured score could be from the real pass rate.

What it misses is *how fast* the margin shrinks. It isn't a straight line. Doubling your questions doesn't cut the margin in half. The margin follows the square root of the number of questions. A square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original. For example, the square root of 400 is 20.

So with 200 questions, the margin only drops from about 10 points to about 7 points. That's better, but it isn't the 5 you wanted. A "point" here means one question in every 100.

To actually halve the margin, you need four times the questions. Going from 100 to 400 takes you from about 10 points off to about 5 points off. Doubling the questions only gets you part of the way.

"About 400 questions" is better because halving the margin takes four times the examples, not twice as many.

check:2:2.a:
"About 110 questions" gets one thing right. More questions do shrink the margin of error, which is how far your score could be from the real pass rate. So adding questions is the right move.

What it misses is how slowly the margin shrinks. Ten extra questions barely help. The lesson's rule says the margin is 100 divided by the square root of the number of questions. A square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives your number. The square root of 100 is 10, so 100 questions gives a margin of about 10 points.

The square root of 110 is only about 10.5. So 100 divided by that is still about 9.5 points. You would still be nearly 10 points off, nowhere near 5.

To get a square root of 20, you need 400 questions, because 20 times 20 is 400. Then 100 divided by 20 gives 5 points.

"About 400 questions" is better because halving the margin takes four times the examples, not just a few more.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Run the margin rule backwards” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem.** "An eval score is only a guess at the real pass rate. With few examples, the margin of error is wide. That's how far off the score could be, either way. Score 70% on 25 questions, and the real rate could be anywhere from 50% to 90%."

**The idea.** "So I run the rule backwards, before testing anything. I pick the smallest improvement I need to detect. That becomes my target margin. Then I work out how many examples give it. The margin shrinks with the square root of the set size, so halving it takes four times the examples. A 5-point margin needs about 400." (A square root is the number that, times itself, gives the original: 20 × 20 = 400.)

**The edge case.** "These numbers assume scores near 50%, the worst case, so they're safe for planning. Near 0% or 100% the rule breaks down. There I'd use a Wilson interval."

**Likely follow-up:** "What if you can't afford four times the examples?"

*Hint:* Compare both versions on the same examples. That is more sensitive, so smaller gains show up without a bigger set. Also log the set size and margin with every MLflow run.

judge.notes: No real problems; the answer matches the lesson. It is about 205 words in total, right at the length limit, though the spoken part itself is shorter.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Scores that wobble.** You rerun almost the same prompt and the pass rate jumps from 72% to 64% to 78%. On a small eval set, that swing is just noise, meaning random luck in which questions happened to pass.
- **Tiny "wins" on few examples.** Prompt B beats prompt A by 4 points on 40 questions, and you call it better. With 40 questions the margin is far wider than 4 points.
- **Great in testing, worse in real use.** You picked the prompt that scored highest on a small set. Real users then see a lower pass rate. It was never really better. It got lucky.
- **Bare scores in MLflow.** Runs show a pass rate but no `n_examples` or `margin_points`. Nobody can tell whether a difference between runs means anything.

**Quickest check**

Take the number of examples and find its square root (the number that, multiplied by itself, gives it). Divide 100 by that. This is your margin in points. Now compare it to the improvement you saw. If the improvement is smaller than the margin, you haven't shown a real change yet.

learn:stops.a:
The "100 divided by the square root of the number of examples" rule is a good planning tool. But it rests on a few assumptions. Here are three places it bends.

**Scores near 0% or 100%.** If your app passes 49 of 50, the rule gives a range that can spill past 100%. That makes no sense. Use a Wilson interval instead. It is a formula built to stay sensible near the edges, and it comes two lessons from now.

**Examples that aren't really separate.** The rule assumes each question is its own independent test. In a RAG app (one that looks up documents before answering), ten questions about the same document tend to pass or fail together. So they count for less than ten. Spread questions across many sources, or use the bootstrap and draw whole groups of related questions at once.

**Real questions that change over time.** A small margin only means you measured this eval set well. If users start asking about new topics, the score can be precise and still misleading. Refresh the set with recent real questions, and log its version (like `faq-v4`) with each MLflow run.

judge.notes: Minor: the 'draw whole groups' bootstrap tweak and the independence assumption go beyond the lesson (though they are statistically sound), and each point runs about four sentences instead of two or three.

learn:term.q: What does “margin of error” mean here?
learn:term.a:
**Margin of error** is how far your measured score might be from the true score, in either direction.

Think of tasting soup. One spoonful gives you a fair idea of the whole pot. But it might have caught an extra salty bit. Taste more spoonfuls and your guess gets closer to how the pot really tastes. One spoonful gives a rough guess. Many spoonfuls give a tight one.

Your eval set works the same way. Each question is a spoonful. The "whole pot" is every question your app will ever face. The pass rate you measure is a guess about that bigger picture.

In the lesson's example, you score 70% on 100 questions. The margin is about 10 **points** (a point is one question in every 100). So the real pass rate is probably somewhere from 60% to 80%. With only 25 questions, the margin grows to about 20 points. With 400 questions, it shrinks to about 5.

That is also why the MLflow snippet logs `margin_points` with each run. A score is only meaningful alongside how far off it could be.

judge.notes: No real problems. The opening definition comes before the soup comparison and one spoonful is called both a fair idea and a rough guess, but these are minor.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The new prompt is no better than the old one”?
check:0:0.a:
"The new prompt is no better" gets one thing right: the test **did not find** a difference. That part is true.

What it misses is the gap between "we didn't see a difference" and "there is no difference." Those are not the same claim. A test can only notice differences that are big enough for the number of examples it has. This is its **power**, meaning the chance it notices a real gain if one exists.

With 40 examples, power is low. Using the lesson's quick rule at a pass rate near 70%, 40 examples per group would only reliably notice a gain of roughly 29 points. A real 5- or 10-point gain could easily hide in the noise. So "no difference found" is what you'd expect even if the new prompt really is better.

Dropping the idea on this result treats a weak test as strong proof.

"40 examples may be too few to notice a gain" is better because it honestly says the test was too small to answer the question, so the right next step is a bigger test, not a final verdict.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The old prompt is better and should stay”?
check:0:2.a:
"The old prompt is better and should stay" gets one thing partly right. If you have to ship something today, keeping the old prompt is a safe choice. Nothing showed the new one is better yet.

But it claims something the test never showed. The test found *no real difference*. That is not the same as finding the old prompt *better*. To say "better," you'd need the old prompt to win clearly, and it didn't.

It also misses the bigger problem: **power**, the chance a test notices a difference that really exists. With only 40 examples, power is very low. Using the lesson's quick rule, a pass rate near 70% needs about 336 examples in each group just to notice a 10-point gain. Forty examples can only catch huge gains. A real but modest improvement could easily hide in the noise. So "no difference" here mostly means "this test was too small to tell."

"40 examples may be too few to notice a gain" is better because it reads the result honestly: the test was too small to judge, so it can't settle which prompt is better.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Any gain at all, even 1 point”?
check:1:1.a:
It's natural to want to catch every improvement. Even a 1-point gain is real progress, so the instinct behind this answer is good.

The problem is what your test can actually see. With about 340 examples in each group, your test only has good **power** (a good chance of noticing a real difference) for bigger gains. Using the lesson's quick rule at a 70% pass rate, noticing a 1-point gain would need about 33,600 examples in each group. That's roughly 100 times what you have.

So if you go looking for a 1-point gain with 340 examples, the test will almost always say "no real difference," even when B really is a bit better. That result isn't evidence that nothing changed. It only means the test was too small to tell. You'd likely end up dropping an improvement that was real.

"A gain of about 10 points or more" is better because the quick rule says a 10-point gain needs about 336 examples in each group, which matches the roughly 340 you can get.

check:1:2.q: Why not “A gain of about 5 points”?
check:1:2.a:
"A gain of about 5 points" gets one thing right: a 5-point gain is real and worth caring about. Wanting to catch it makes sense.

The problem is the numbers. At a pass rate near 70%, the quick rule says noticing a 5-point gain takes about 1,344 examples in each group. You only have about 340. That's roughly a quarter of what you need.

With that few examples, the test has low **power**. Power is the chance the test notices a difference that really exists. Here it would often come back saying "no real difference" even if version B truly is 5 points better. The gain is just too small to see through the random ups and downs of 340 examples. You'd spend the effort and likely learn nothing you could trust.

The lesson's advice applies: if you can't get enough examples for the small difference, look only for bigger ones.

"A gain of about 10 points or more" is better because it needs about 336 examples a group, which your 340 covers, so the test has a fair chance of noticing it.

check:2:0.a:
"About twice as many" gets one thing right: a smaller gain is harder to spot, so you do need more examples. The instinct points the right way.

What it misses is that the difference appears **twice** in the quick rule. You divide by the difference times itself. So when the gain shrinks to half, the bottom of the fraction shrinks to half of a half, which is one quarter. Dividing by one quarter makes the answer four times bigger, not two.

The lesson's own numbers show this. At a 70% pass rate:

- noticing a 10-point gain takes about 336 examples per group
- noticing a 5-point gain takes about 1,344 per group

That is 336 × 4, not 336 × 2. If you only doubled to 672, your test would have low **power**. Power is the chance the test notices a real difference. With too little power, you'd often get "no real difference" even when version B truly is better.

"About four times as many" is better because halving the difference shrinks "the difference times itself" to a quarter, which multiplies the examples you need by four.

check:2:2.a:
"About the same number" gets one thing right. The top part of the quick rule, 16 times the pass rate times (1 minus the pass rate), doesn't change. Your pass rate is still around 70%, so that part stays put.

What it misses is the bottom part. You divide by the difference times itself. That squaring is the key. If you halve the difference, the bottom becomes half times half, which is a quarter of what it was. Dividing by something a quarter as big gives an answer four times as big.

You can see this in the lesson's numbers. Noticing a 10-point gain at 70% takes about 336 examples per group. Noticing a 5-point gain, half the size, takes about 1,344. That is four times as many, not about the same.

The intuition: a smaller difference is harder to see, and it hides in the random noise faster than you'd guess. With the same number of examples, your test would often say "no real difference" even when there was one.

"About four times as many" is better because halving the difference shrinks the squared bottom of the rule to a quarter, which multiplies the examples needed by four.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The explanation matches the lesson's numbers (336 → 1,344), and the length is borderline at about 200 words.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Size the test before running it” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "If I compare two versions on too few examples, a real improvement can hide in random ups and downs. The test says 'no difference' when there actually was one."

*The idea:* "So before running anything, I pick the smallest gain worth finding, say 5 points on a 70% pass rate. Then I work out how many examples each version needs for about an 80% chance of noticing that gain. That chance is called the test's power. For 5 points it's roughly 1,344 examples per group. For 10 points, about 336."

*The trade-off:* "Halving the gain I want to detect roughly quadruples the examples needed. If I can't get that many, I only look for bigger gains. Or I run a paired comparison on the same examples, which usually needs fewer."

**A likely follow-up**

"Your test found no difference. Does that mean the two versions are equally good?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Say no. It only means there was no difference bigger than the test was sized to see. Point back to the planned sample size and power before drawing any conclusion.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
The warning signs usually show up in results that don't hold steady.

**What you might see:**

- A comparison says "no real difference," but version B clearly does better once real users try it. The test was too small to notice the gain.
- You rerun the same comparison on a fresh batch of examples and the winner flips. Small groups make results jumpy.
- A gap of 3 or 4 points gets waved off as noise, again and again. That can mean the test never had the size to notice it.
- Your eval set is small, say 100 or 200 examples, yet the team is chasing 5-point gains.
- In MLflow, the run has no logged `examples_per_group` value. That suggests nobody sized the test before running it.
- The "smallest difference worth finding" was chosen after looking at the results, not before.

**Quickest check:**

Take your current pass rate and the smallest gain you care about. Plug them into the lesson's quick rule. Then compare that number to how many examples each version actually got. If you had far fewer, the test's "no difference" verdict tells you very little.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The pass rate is near 0% or 100%.** The quick rule is a rough shortcut, and it gets less reliable when, say, 97% of examples already pass. Use the exact calculation from `statsmodels` instead. Also check whether a few more passes would even matter to users.

**2. An LLM is doing the grading, or the app itself is random.** The rule assumes each example gives one clean pass or fail. But an LLM app can answer differently each run, and an LLM judge (a model that scores answers) makes its own mistakes. Both add noise, so you need more examples. Run each example a few times, and spot-check the judge against human labels.

**3. Your examples aren't really separate.** Fifty questions about the same document tend to pass or fail together. They teach you less than fifty unrelated questions would, so your real count is smaller than it looks. Spread examples across many sources. If the same examples go through both versions, size the test by how often the two versions disagree, as in "Comparing on the same examples".

judge.notes: Minor: points 2 and 3 run past the requested two or three sentences each. Content is accurate and consistent with the lesson.

learn:term.a:
"Before" means **before you run the comparison and look at any results**. You make the plan first, then collect the data.

Think of baking a cake. You decide how long it bakes and check the recipe *before* it goes in the oven. If you only decide once you see it, you'll be tempted to call whatever came out "done."

Tests work the same way. If you peek at the results first, it's easy to pick a difference size that makes your result look good. Deciding up front keeps the test honest.

So, before running anything, you settle two things:

1. The smallest difference worth finding, like a 5-point gain.
2. How many examples each group needs to have a fair chance of noticing it.

You can see this in the lesson's example. The math uses only a guessed pass rate (about 70%) and the gain you hope to spot. No real results go in. The same is true in the `statsmodels` code: `solve_power` works out the number, and `mlflow.log_param` saves it as a plan, all before either version is tested.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The smaller chunk size helped”?
check:0:0.a:
"The smaller chunk size helped" is a natural guess. It gets one thing right: you did change `chunk_size` (how big each piece of a document is when it's split up for searching), and run B did score 6 points higher. The smaller chunks *might* be the reason.

What it misses is the second change. Run B also used index `v8` instead of `v7`. The index is the searchable copy of your documents. Maybe `v8` has new or cleaner documents. That alone could explain the 6 points.

So there are several possible stories:

- The smaller chunks helped.
- The new index helped.
- Both helped a bit.
- The smaller chunks actually hurt, but the new index helped even more.

The two runs can't tell these apart. Picking "the smaller chunk size helped" claims an answer the data doesn't support. That's what a confound does: it turns the result into non-evidence.

"Nothing yet: rerun B on index v7" is better because it admits you can't tell yet, and it fixes the problem by making `chunk_size` the only thing that differs between the runs.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Index v8 helped, so switch to it”?
check:0:2.a:
"Index v8 helped" gets one thing right: it notices that the index changed, and that change might matter.

But it jumps to a conclusion. Two things changed between run A and run B. First, `chunk_size` went from 512 to 256. That setting controls how big each piece of text is when the documents are cut up. Second, the index went from `v7` to `v8`. The index is the searchable copy of the documents that the app looks things up in.

The 6-point gain could come from the smaller chunks, the new index, or both together. It is even possible that `v8` made things worse and the smaller chunks made up for it. Giving all the credit to the index is a guess, not a finding. This result shows only that the two changes together scored higher.

"Nothing yet: rerun B on index v7" is better because it puts the index back to match run A, which leaves `chunk_size` as the only difference, so the next result actually means something.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A fair test: the name stayed the same”?
check:1:1.a:
"A fair test: the name stayed the same" gets one thing right. On paper, the runs do match. MLflow shows the same settings for A and B, including the same model name. So if you only look at the logged parameters, it looks fair.

What it misses is that a name is just a label. The provider can swap the actual model behind that label at any time. Your logs said the model stayed the same, but the thing doing the answering changed. A fair test needs the real controls to match, not just their labels.

So the lower score in run B is not evidence about anything you did. It might be the new model. You can't tell, because a setting moved that you didn't plan and didn't record.

The lesson's fix applies here. Log a pinned version of the model, meaning a specific dated release that won't change under you, not just its general name. Then a swap would show up when you compare the two runs' settings.

"A confound: a control quietly moved" is better because it names what really happened: something you meant to hold steady changed without you knowing, so the comparison no longer counts.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'specific dated release that won't change under you' wording goes slightly beyond the lesson, which only says to log the model version, and the length is right at the limit.

check:1:2.q: Why not “A bug in how MLflow logs runs”?
check:1:2.a:
It's a fair first guess. MLflow showed two runs with matching settings, yet the scores were very different. So it's natural to suspect the record-keeping.

But MLflow did its job. It logged exactly what it was given. Both runs really did use the same model *name*, so the logged value really was the same. Nothing was recorded wrongly.

The change happened outside your code and outside MLflow. The provider (the company that serves the model) swapped the model behind that name. Run B used different model behaviour from run A. That's a second thing that changed without you planning it. That's the definition of a confound.

The lesson here is not "MLflow is broken." It's "I didn't log a setting that mattered." The name alone wasn't enough. Logging a pinned version would have shown the difference. A pinned version is a specific dated model ID instead of a general name.

"A confound: a control quietly moved" is better because it names the real problem. An unplanned change outside your code means the score gap tells you nothing about anything you did.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the 'pinned dated model ID' explanation goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Rebuild the index before every run”?
check:2:0.a:
"Rebuild the index before every run" sounds careful, and it does get one thing right. Each run gets a clean, complete index (the searchable copy of the documents), with nothing half-built or stale.

The problem is what goes into each rebuild. New documents arrive every day, so a rebuild on Monday and a rebuild on Friday hold different documents. The index quietly changes between runs. That is a confound: a second thing that changed without you planning it.

Say run B scores better than run A. Was it your planned change, like `chunk_size`? Or were the answers just in the new documents? You can't tell. You end up measuring the documents, not your change.

Being up to date matters for a live app. In an experiment, it works against you. What you need is for everything except your one planned change to stay exactly the same.

Building the index once from a fixed copy is better because every run then searches the same documents, under one logged version like `index=v7`, so any difference in results comes from the one thing you changed.

judge.notes: Minor: the 'clean, complete index' and 'up to date matters for a live app' points come from outside the lesson, but they do not contradict it.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Only run on days with no new files”?
check:2:1.a:
**It gets one thing right.** It notices that new documents are a confound, a second change that could explain the difference instead of the change you planned.

**But it doesn't actually stop the documents from changing.** Say run A happens on a quiet day in week one, and run B on a quiet day in week two. Each day had no new files. But files arrived on the days in between. So the two runs still searched different sets of documents. You'd be measuring the documents, not your change.

**It also puts your experiment at the mercy of luck.** If files arrive every day, you may get very few quiet days, or none at all. Then you can't run the experiment.

**Why "Build the index once from a fixed copy" is better:** freezing one copy of the documents, giving that index a version, and logging the version with every run keeps the documents identical across all runs, no matter what arrives during the two weeks. (The index is the searchable copy of your documents that the app looks things up in.)

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare two dicts key by key” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "A comparison between two runs only counts as evidence if the one thing I planned to change is the only thing that changed. Any other setting that moved is a confound, a hidden second cause."

*The idea.* "I treat each run's settings as a dict, a list of name–value pairs. I walk through every name that appears in either run. I skip the one I planned to change. I flag any name whose values differ, and I sort the flagged names so the report is easy to read."

*The edge case.* "A setting that is missing from one run still counts as a difference. If run B logged `judge` and run A didn't, I can't prove they match, so I flag it."

**Likely follow-up**

"What if two values look different but mean the same thing?"

*Hint:* MLflow stores parameters as text. So `5` and `5.0`, or `0.50` and `0.5`, won't match. A strong answer has two parts. First, log every setting in one consistent format. Second, decide on purpose whether to clean values up before comparing. Flagging too much is safer than missing a real confound.

judge.notes: No major problems. The claim that MLflow stores parameters as text is not in the lesson, though it does not contradict it. The answer also retells the comparison steps in words, but it gives no code and no Check answer.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A big jump from a small change.** You nudged `chunk_size` and the score leapt. Tiny changes rarely cause huge effects. Something else probably moved.
- **The win won't repeat.** You rerun the "better" version later and the gain shrinks or vanishes.
- **Your baseline drifts.** You rerun the old, unchanged version and get a different score than before. The setup moved under you.
- **The eval looks different.** The question count changed, or every answer's score shifted at once, which points to a new judge model (the model that grades answers).
- **It fails in real use.** The score looked great, then dropped once real users arrived. The test conditions didn't match reality.

**Quickest check**

Open both runs in MLflow and compare their logged parameters side by side. Only the one setting you planned should differ. Watch for settings logged in one run but missing from the other.

If a setting was never logged, like the index version or judge version, you can't rule it out. Treat the result as unproven. Then rerun both versions on the same frozen setup.

learn:stops.a:
**When this stops working**

**1. The setting looks the same, but isn't.** A provider can update the model behind the same name, like `gpt-4o`. Your parameter diff shows no change, yet answers shift. Pin a dated model version where you can, and log the exact version string the provider returns.

**2. A setting was never logged.** The diff only sees what you logged. A prompt edited in a file, a new library version, or a changed system message stays invisible. Log every setting that could matter, including package versions and a fingerprint of the prompt text. A fingerprint (called a hash) is a short code that changes whenever the text changes.

**3. Only one thing changed, but the result is still noisy.** With temperature above zero, or a small eval set, two runs of the *same* setup can score differently. The gap you see might just be chance. Repeat each run a few times, use a larger eval set, and only trust differences bigger than that run-to-run wobble.

learn:term.a:
A **confound** is a second thing that changed between two runs without you planning it.

**An everyday comparison.** Say you try a new plant food to see if your plant grows faster. That same week, you also move the pot to a sunnier window. The plant grows faster. Was it the food or the sun? You can't tell. The sun is the confound. It moved quietly, and now your result says nothing clear about the food.

**In the lesson's example.** The planned change is `chunk_size`, which is how big each piece of a document is when it gets stored. Run A uses `512` and run B uses `256`. So far, so good.

Now look at the other settings:

- `k` (how many pieces get looked up) is `5` in both runs, so it matches.
- `judge` (the model that grades answers) is `j2` in both runs, so it matches.
- `index` (the searchable copy of the documents) is `v7` in run A but `v8` in run B.

That `index` difference is the confound. If run B scores better, the cause could be the smaller chunks or the rebuilt index. The comparison can't settle which one it was.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Ship it: it won clearly on the dev set”?
check:0:0.a:
"Ship it" gets one thing right. A clear win on the dev set is a real signal. That prompt is a good candidate, and it deserves a closer look.

What it misses is how the winner was found. You tried 15 variants. Each comparison has about a 5% chance of a lucky win, called a **false positive**. Across 15 tries, the chance that at least one of them "wins" by luck is roughly half. So the best of 15 is partly the best prompt and partly the luckiest one.

Its dev score is also too optimistic. You used the dev set (the examples you test against while choosing) to pick the winner. A score from the same examples you used to choose will flatter your pick. A clear margin doesn't fix this. Luck can produce clear margins too.

"Confirm it once on the holdout set" is better because the holdout examples were kept aside and never seen, so a single fresh test shows whether the win is real or just the luck of picking the best of many.

judge.notes: No significant problems; 'roughly half' for 15 variants is about 54%, which fits between the lesson's 40% for 10 and 64% for 20.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Try 15 more variants to be sure”?
check:0:2.a:
"Try 15 more variants to be sure" gets one thing right. It doesn't trust a single win, and that caution is good.

But it adds evidence in the wrong direction. Each new variant is one more comparison, and each comparison has its own 5% chance of a lucky win. With 15 variants, the chance that at least one "won" by luck is already about 54%, roughly a coin flip. Going to 30 pushes it near 79%. You'd end up with a winner you can trust *less*, not more.

It also keeps using the dev set, the examples you've been tuning against. Picking the best of many on the same examples makes that score too optimistic. More tries on the same data only deepens the problem.

What you actually need is a fresh, fair test the winner has never seen. That's the job of the holdout set: examples kept aside and not used while you search.

**Confirm it once on the holdout set** is better because it gives a single, unbiased check on new data, so a lucky win on dev gets caught instead of shipped.

check:1:0.q: Why not “20 prompts is too few to try”?
check:1:0.a:
"20 prompts is too few to try" does notice something real. The number of prompts matters. But it gets the direction backwards.

The lesson's table shows why. Each comparison has a 5% chance of a **false positive**, meaning a prompt that looks like a winner only by luck. Try 1 prompt and that risk is 5%. Try 20 and the chance that at least one wins by luck is about 64%. Trying more prompts raises the fluke risk. So "try more" would make the teammate's problem worse.

That option also misses the real mistake. The teammate picked the best prompt using the dev set. Then they quoted its score on that same dev set. The best of many is partly luck, so that score is too optimistic. It is not a fair guess for production.

The fix is to limit how many prompts you test. Then confirm the winner **once** on the holdout set. That is the set of examples kept aside, which the winner has never seen.

"The best of 20 is partly luck" is better because it names the real problem: the winner's dev-set score is inflated by luck, so it overstates what production will show.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Dev-set scores always run low”?
check:1:1.a:
"Dev-set scores always run low" gets one thing right. The quoted dev-set score is not a safe forecast for production. (The dev set is the examples you used while trying and comparing prompts.)

But it has the direction backwards. The teammate's score is more likely too **high**, not too low.

Here's why. Each prompt's score has some luck in it. Some prompts get a lucky bump on these particular examples. When you try 20 and keep the top one, you tend to pick a prompt that is good *and* got lucky. That luck won't repeat on new data, so real performance usually drops.

The word "always" is also a problem. Dev-set scores don't run low as a rule. The trouble comes from *choosing the best of many*, not from the dev set itself.

So the fix isn't to bump the number up. It's to test the winner **once** on the holdout set. That is the set of examples kept aside that the winner has never seen.

"The best of 20 is partly luck" is better because it names the real cause: picking the top of many scores makes the winner look better than it really is.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Run all 50 on the holdout set”?
check:2:0.a:
"Run all 50 on the holdout set" gets one thing right. The holdout set is the honest test, because it holds examples the prompts have never seen.

The problem is how many times you use it. Each comparison has about a 5% chance of a lucky win. Across 50 comparisons, the chance that at least one prompt "wins" by luck is about 92%. Running all 50 on the holdout just moves the fluke problem there. You would still pick the best of 50, and its score would still be too optimistic.

Then the holdout is used up. Nothing clean is left to confirm the winner on. Its whole job is one final check of one winner.

"Test fewer, with a stricter threshold" is better because it cuts the number of chances for luck before any test runs, and it makes each chance harder to win: you share the usual 5% across all your comparisons, so each one must clear a much higher bar.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Run each idea once to save money”?
check:2:2.a:
Saving money is a fair goal, and running each idea once is not wrong in itself. But it does not guard against the problem this lesson is about.

The risk comes from **how many comparisons** you make, not how many times you run each one. A comparison means checking one prompt against the baseline (your current version). Each one carries a 5% chance of a **false positive**, a "win" that is really just luck. Run 50 ideas once each and you still make 50 comparisons. The fluke risk is exactly the same as before; you have only cut the bill.

The table shows the chance of at least one lucky winner is already 64% with 20 variants. With 50 it climbs higher still. So the plan saves money but leaves you just as likely to crown a fluke.

**"Test fewer, with a stricter threshold" is better because it shrinks the number of chances for luck and makes each lucky win harder to get.** For example, with 10 variants the Bonferroni correction (dividing 5% by the number of comparisons) asks each to pass at 0.5%.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Chance of at least one fluke” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem:** "Every comparison has a small chance of a false positive. That means a variant looks better purely by luck. At the usual 95% standard, that chance is 5% per test."

**The idea:** "Those small chances add up. Each extra test is another chance for a fluke, so the odds that *every* test stays clean keep shrinking. With 20 variants, there's about a 64% chance at least one 'wins' by luck. It's like rolling a die. One roll rarely gives a six, but roll enough and a six turns up."

**The trade-off:** "You can guard against this with the Bonferroni correction. That means dividing the 5% by the number of tests, so 20 tests means 0.25% each. It's safer, but it's strict. A real but small improvement may fail to pass."

**A likely follow-up**

*"So how do you trust the winner you picked?"*

Hint: Point to the holdout set. That's a batch of examples kept aside, which no variant was tuned on. Confirm the winner there **once**. Its score on the dev set is too optimistic, because the best of many is partly luck. The holdout score is the honest one.

judge.notes: No real problems. The phrase "those small chances add up" is loose, since they compound rather than sum, but it does not contradict the lesson. "Dev set" is also not explained.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The winner's score drops later.** It looked great on the dev set, then sinks on the holdout set or with real users. That gap is the luck wearing off.
- **The win is small.** The best prompt beat your current version by a hair, after many tries. Tiny wins found after a long search are often flukes.
- **Lots of tries, one reported.** Your `prompt-search` experiment holds dozens of `dev` runs, but only the best score made it into the report.
- **The holdout set was used more than once.** Several runs tagged `holdout`, or prompts tweaked after peeking at holdout scores. Once you tune against it, it is no longer "unseen". The holdout set is the batch of examples kept aside for the final check.

**Quickest check**

Open the experiment in MLflow. Count the `dev` runs. That number is how many comparisons you made.

Then find the winner's `holdout` run. Confirm three things:

1. It exists.
2. There is only one.
3. Its score is close to the dev score.

For a stricter check, divide 5% by that count. This is the Bonferroni correction. Then ask whether the win still clears the tougher bar.

learn:stops.a:
The rule assumes a few things. Here is where it needs extra care.

**1. You peek at the holdout more than once.** The holdout only works while the winner has never seen it. If you check it after every tweak, it quietly becomes another set of examples you tune against, and its score turns optimistic too. Use it once, and when you need a fresh check, gather new holdout examples.

**2. Your app's answers vary from run to run.** An LLM can give different outputs for the same input, so one eval run can look good by chance. Run each variant a few times and compare the averages, not a single lucky score.

**3. You have very little data.** With a tiny holdout set, a few examples can swing the score a lot. Collect more examples first, or treat any "win" as a hint rather than proof.

learn:term.a:
They aren't two of the same kind of thing. **Design** is a *stage* of your work. **Bonferroni** is one *tool* you can use during that stage.

**Design** is the planning step, before you run anything. You decide what to test and how many variants to try. The lesson's first guard lives here: keep the number of variants small. Fewer comparisons means fewer chances for a lucky "win."

**Bonferroni** is a specific rule you can apply while designing. You take the usual 5% fluke allowance and divide it by the number of comparisons. Each test then has to clear a much higher bar.

How they work together, using the lesson's table:

- Test 20 variants at the normal 5% bar, and there's about a 64% chance one wins by luck.
- Design says: do you really need 20? Cutting to 5 lowers the risk to 23%.
- Bonferroni says: if you keep 20, make each one beat 0.25% (5% ÷ 20) instead of 5%.

Think of planning a party. Design is deciding how many guests to invite. Bonferroni is a stricter dress code you set because the guest list is long.

check:0:0.q: Why not “A is better: it won 12 of the 20”?
check:0:0.a:
That answer gets one thing right. It looks only at the 20 disagreements, not all 200 questions. That is the correct place to look, because the 180 examples where A and B agree tell you nothing about which is better.

What it misses is luck. A won 12 and B won 8, so the gap is 4. Imagine A and B were exactly as good as each other. Then each disagreement would be like a coin flip. Flip a coin 20 times and getting 12 heads is very common. It does not mean the coin is unfair.

The lesson's quick rule says that with 20 disagreements the gap needs to be about 9 or more. That is the point where the result is **statistically significant**, meaning too big to be luck. A gap of 4 is well below that line. So "A is better" claims more than the evidence supports.

"Too close to call on 20 disagreements" is the better answer because it checks the gap of 4 against the needed gap of about 9 and admits that a 12 to 8 split could easily be luck.

check:0:2.q: Why not “B is better: 8 wins is a fair share”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. It looks at the **disagreements**, the 20 questions where only one setup passed. That is where the useful information is.

But it draws the wrong conclusion in two ways.

First, it points the wrong way. B won 8 and A won 12. If either setup were ahead, it would be A, not B. Winning "a fair share" is not the same as winning more.

Second, it skips the luck check. With 20 disagreements, the gap between the two counts needs to be about 9 or more before you can call it real. Here the gap is 12 minus 8, which is 4. That is well below 9. A split like 12 to 8 happens easily by chance, like flipping a coin 20 times and getting 12 heads. So neither A nor B has shown it is better.

"Too close to call on 20 disagreements" is better because it compares the gap of 4 against the needed gap of about 9 and honestly says the difference could be luck.

check:1:0.a:
"All 100 questions" sounds fair, and it gets one thing right. You did need to run both setups on all 100. That is what makes this a paired comparison, meaning each question is checked for A and B side by side. Without the full run, you couldn't know which questions they agree on.

But once you look at the results, the 90 agreements stop helping. If both passed a question, it was easy for both. If both failed, it was hard for both. Either way, that question says nothing about which setup is better. It's a draw, and draws don't pick a winner.

Counting all 100 also hides the real signal. A gap of a few wins looks tiny next to 100. Next to 10, you can see whether it's a clear lead or a near-even split. That is why McNemar's test, the standard check for pass/fail results, ignores the agreements completely.

"The 10 where they disagree" is better because those are the only questions where one setup did something the other couldn't.

check:1:1.a:
It's a natural pick. The 90 agreements are most of your data, so it feels like they should carry the most weight.

And they do tell you something. They show how good both setups are in general. If both pass most of those 90, both are decent. If both fail many, both struggle.

But they can't tell you which one is **better**. On each of those 90 questions, A and B got the same result. Either both passed or both failed. A question where they tie gives neither side a point. You could delete all 90, and the contest between A and B would stand exactly where it was.

This is also why a paired comparison (running both setups on the same questions) works so well. A hard question trips up both setups, so it lands in the "agree" pile. Its difficulty cancels out instead of muddying the result.

"The 10 where they disagree" is the right answer because those are the only questions where one setup won and the other lost, so only they can show which one is ahead.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Run each one more time”?
check:2:1.a:
"Run each one more time" sounds sensible, and it gets one thing right. Running again gives you more results, and that can smooth out random wobble. (Models can answer a bit differently each time, so one run might be lucky or unlucky.)

But it misses the key requirement. If A runs again on its own questions and B runs again on its own, they are still on **different** questions. A paired comparison needs to line up each question with both answers side by side: A's result and B's result on `q1`, then on `q2`, and so on.

Without that, you can't find the disagreements, the questions where one passed and the other failed. You also lose the big benefit of pairing. A hard question should be hard for both setups, so its difficulty cancels out. On separate question sets, one setup might simply have drawn easier questions, and extra runs won't fix that.

"Run both on the same questions" is the right answer, because it gives every question a result from A and from B, so you can count the disagreements and check whether the gap is real.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Use a bigger judge model”?
check:2:2.a:
A bigger judge model is a fair instinct, but it fixes the wrong problem.

A "judge model" is the AI that grades each answer as pass or fail. A bigger one might grade more accurately. That has some value: fewer grading mistakes means cleaner scores.

But grading isn't what's blocking a paired comparison here. The trouble is that A and B answered *different* questions. A paired comparison works by lining up the two setups example by example and counting only the disagreements, where one passed and the other failed. With separate question sets, there is nothing to line up. Question 7 for A has no matching question 7 for B.

So even a perfect judge leaves you with two overall scores on two different sets. One set might simply be easier. That difference in difficulty doesn't cancel out, and you can't count disagreements at all.

**"Run both on the same questions"** is better because shared questions are what make pairing possible, letting you count the disagreements and run McNemar's test.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Count only the disagreements” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* Setup A scores higher than setup B on an eval set, a fixed set of test questions. Is the difference real, or just luck?

*The idea.* Run both setups on the same examples and compare them one example at a time. If both pass, or both fail, that example tells you nothing. Only the disagreements count: A passed and B failed, or the other way round. The "gap" is A's wins minus B's wins on those disagreements. McNemar's test, the standard check for pass/fail results, says how big the gap must be. With 20 disagreements, it must be about 9. So 15 to 5 (gap 10) is a real win. 12 to 8 (gap 4) is too close to call.

*The edge case.* With fewer than about 25 disagreements, that rough threshold is too generous. A 5-to-0 split passes it, but the exact version of the test says it could still be luck.

**Likely follow-up:** "Why not just compare the two overall scores?"

**Hint:** A hard example is hard for both setups. Pairing cancels out that shared difficulty, so the comparison is much more sensitive.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A "win" that vanishes.** You switch to the new prompt, and real-world quality looks the same. The gap was luck all along.
- **Only overall scores in your logs.** Your MLflow run shows "A: 82%, B: 78%" but no `a_only` and `b_only` counts. That means nobody looked at the disagreements.
- **The two setups ran on different examples.** For instance, B ran on an older eval set or a random sample. Hard examples no longer cancel out, so the comparison is unfair.
- **Rows that don't line up.** The same question has a different answer than you expect in A's list versus B's. The lists were shuffled or filtered differently, so you are comparing q2 against q7.
- **A winner from very few disagreements.** Something like 5 to 0 gets called significant, which means "too big to be luck." The quick rule is too generous below about 25 disagreements.

**Quickest check**

Open both result lists side by side. Confirm each row is the same example ID. Then count the disagreements and the gap. Ask yourself: is the gap at least about twice the square root of the disagreement count? If not, call it a tie.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the rule needs extra care.

**Very few disagreements.** Below about 25 disagreements, the quick "gap squared versus 4 times disagreements" rule is too generous. A 5 to 0 split passes it but could still be luck. Use the exact version of McNemar's test, or better, add more examples before deciding.

**LLM answers that change between runs.** An LLM can give a different answer to the same question each time. So one example might pass, then fail on a rerun. Some "disagreements" are just noise. Run each setup a few times per example, or set temperature (the randomness setting) to 0, and treat examples that flip as unreliable.

**Many comparisons on one eval set.** If you test 20 prompt tweaks against the same set, one will look "significant" by luck alone. You have also quietly tuned your prompts to that set. Confirm the winner on a fresh held-out set, meaning examples you never looked at while tuning.

judge.notes: No real problems. The small-sample point matches the lesson. The other two points go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it. The answer only names the gap-squared rule that the lesson already states and does not write the solution.

learn:term.a:
"Paired" means each example gives you a pair of results: one from A and one from B, on the exact same input.

Here's an everyday picture. Two friends take the same quiz. Instead of only comparing final scores, you go through it question by question. If a question was a trick question, both probably missed it. That tells you nothing about who is better. What matters are the questions one friend got right and the other got wrong.

That is the point of pairing. A hard example is hard for both setups, so its difficulty cancels out. You are comparing A and B under identical conditions.

In the lesson's table, each row is one pair:

- `q1` (both ✓) and `q4` (both ✗) are agreements, so you ignore them.
- `q2` is "A only" and `q3` is "B only." These disagreements are the only rows you count.

Then you compare the two counts. With 20 disagreements, 15 to 5 is a gap of 10. That is big enough to say A really wins. A split of 12 to 8 is a gap of only 4, which is too close to rule out luck.

But adding only works if you change one setting at a time and leave the others alone. A full grid search tries every combination. Each chunk size is paired with every value of k. Each of those pairs is then tried with every model.

Build it up step by step:

- 4 chunk sizes, each with 5 values of k, gives 4 × 5 = 20 pairs.
- Each of those 20 pairs runs with 3 models, which gives 20 × 3 = 60 runs.

"20" is a good start. It comes from 4 chunk sizes times 5 values of `k`. That is the right move: you multiply, you don't add. Every chunk size gets paired with every `k`, so you get 20 pairs.

What it misses is the third setting, the models. A full grid means every combination of every setting you planned to vary. Each of those 20 pairs still has to be tried with each of the 3 models. So each pair turns into 3 runs.

check:1:0.q: Why not “It goes up by just one run”?
check:1:0.a:
"It goes up by just one run" gets one thing right. You are adding exactly one new value: a single extra model in the model list.

What it misses is how a grid works. A grid search tries every combination of values. So the new model does not get one run. It gets paired with every chunk size and every value of `k`, just like the other two models.

Here is a small example. Say you have 2 chunk sizes and 2 values of `k`. That makes 4 combinations for each model.

- 2 models: 4 times 2 is 8 runs.
- 3 models: 4 times 3 is 12 runs.

Adding one model added 4 runs, not 1. Each of those runs pays for its own eval and judge calls, so the cost grows by the same amount. Think of the outfits idea: adding one more shirt gives you a new outfit for every pair of trousers you own, not just one.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Nothing until the next grid”?
check:1:2.a:
"Nothing until the next grid" gets one small thing right. Runs you have already finished don't change. Their results stay logged in MLflow, untouched.

But it treats the new model as something separate, to be dealt with later. That's not how a grid works. A grid is every combination of the values you listed. The moment the third model joins the list of models, it becomes part of the grid. It has to be paired with every chunk size and every value of `k`, just like the first two models were.

So the number of runs doesn't stay the same. It grows by a whole extra block. If you had 2 chunk sizes and 2 values of `k`, that's 4 combinations per model. Two models meant 8 runs. Three models means 12. Each new run also pays for its own eval and judge calls, so the cost grows by the same amount.

"Every chunk size and k runs again for it" is better because it names exactly what adding a value does: the new model repeats the full set of other combinations, so the run count multiplies instead of staying flat.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The only small point is the claim that finished runs stay logged in MLflow, which the lesson doesn't state outright, though it fits the lesson's MLflow setup.
